newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: India, Pakistan set peace talks for March 28-31.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan set peace talks for March 28-31.

text.p: Pakistan announced on Thursday that it would resume stalled peace talks with arch-rival India on March 28 in New Delhi, where Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda said he expected a positive outcome from the four-day meeting.
A Foreign Ministry statement in Islamabad said the talks between foreign ministry secretaries Shamshad Ahmad of Pakistan and Salman Haider of India would last until March 31.

"Pursuant to the exchange of letters between the prime ministers of Pakistan and India, it has been decided that the foreign secretaries of the two countries will meet in New Delhi on March 28-31," the brief Pakistani announcement said.
In New Delhi, Deve Gowda said earlier he hoped the talks, stalled for more than three years, would yield positive results.

"I hope official-level discussions will give some positive results," he told the upper house of parliament during a debate on his government's economic and political policies. "India is prepared to extend full cooperation to Pakistan."

The last round of talks between the South Asian neighbours was held in January 1994 but they bogged down owing to differences over the disputed Himalayan region of Jammu and Kashmir, the cause of two of their three wars since they gained independence from Britain in 1947.

New Delhi accuses Islamabad of arming and training separatist guerrillas fighting Indian rule over two-thirds of Kashmir. Pakistan, which controls the remaining third of the territory, says it gives them only moral and diplomatic support.
Following Nawaz Sharif's election as Pakistan's prime minister last month, New Delhi and Islamabad have exchanged letters expressing a desire to resume bilateral talks.
Pakistan said on Saturday it was also willing to discuss a troop pullout from the disputed Siachen glacier in northern Kashmir near the Chinese border.

Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral wrote to his Pakistani counterpart, Gohar Ayub Khan, at the weekend, welcoming Pakistan's suggestion that foreign secretaries from the two countries should meet in March to prepare ground for a meeting between their prime ministers.
Pakistan has insisted that the two sides discuss Kashmir. India has said it is keen to narrow differences over less contentious issues to help improve the overall climate between the longtime foes.

"There is no question of any pre-conditions," the Press Trust of India quoted Gujral as saying on Thursday in Mauritius, where he was attending a meeting of foreign ministers from nations ringing the Indian Ocean.
"They (Pakistan) have not stipulated any pre-condition, and we are not ready to accept any."
Sharif had earlier said that the "core issue" of Kashmir would have to be discussed. "We are ready to discuss all subjects," Gujral was quoted as saying.
